meta.descriptionEn: November 2002. A 26-year-old single-hulled tanker carrying 77,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil is battered by a storm off the Coast of Death in Galicia, Spain. Its hull bursts. Then three governments, Spain, France and Portugal, refuse to let it dock. Instead of a sheltered port, the stricken ship is towed back out to sea. Six days later it splits in two. What followed was the worst ecological disaster in Spain's history, more than 2,000 kilometres of polluted coast, and a legal fight that lasted more than a decade and reached courts in New York and London. Who was really to blame: the captain, the owners, the inspectors or the governments? Watch the full story and decide.

Uska hull phat gaya, magar Spain, France aur Portugal ne use apni bandargah mein anay se rok diya. Jahaz ko wapas khuley samandar mein kheench liya gaya, aur chhe din baad woh do tukron mein toot kar doob gaya. Is hadsay ne Spain ki tareekh ka sab se bara mahouliyati nuqsan kiya. articleEn: On 19 November 2002, an old oil tanker called the Prestige broke in two in the sea off the coast of Galicia. It was carrying 77,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil, and that oil was now going to spill into the water. An estimated 60,000 tonnes entered the sea, about 17.8 million US gallons. The oil affected 2,300 kilometres of coastline and more than a thousand beaches. It remains the biggest environmental disaster in the history of both Spain and Portugal.

The central questions are why the tanker stayed at sea for several days, and why France, Spain and Portugal would not let it dock. The most important question is who was responsible: the ship's owner, the classification society, or the decisions made during the storm. The courts spent years on these matters. The first verdict gave the captain only a suspended sentence, and the Supreme Court later changed that ruling. The world was then left to ask what should be done about old tankers like this one, and whether the lesson was really learned.

This is not only the story of one accident. It is the story of an old ship, a warning that was ignored, and difficult decisions made by several countries. So let us begin at the start and follow what happened to the tanker nobody wanted, step by step.

articleEn: First, the ship itself. The Prestige was a single-hulled oil tanker, and at the time of the accident it was 26 years old. Single-hulled means the hull has only one layer. With a double hull, the risk of a spill and its severity are lower. At that time the US and most other countries were planning to phase out single-hulled tankers by 2012, but older ships like the Prestige were still in service.

The ship was Greek-operated but registered in the Bahamas, so it sailed under a Bahamian flag. Ownership was also complicated. The owner was a Liberian-registered single-purpose corporation, which later court cases named as Mare Shipping Inc. This made it hard for investigators to decide who was truly responsible, and it shows the regulatory problems that come with flags of convenience.

The ship's size matters too. Its deadweight tonnage, meaning its carrying capacity, was about 81,000 tons. That put it at the small end of the Aframax class: smaller than most crude oil carriers, but bigger than most refined-products carriers. The American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) was responsible for classification, and it had certified the Prestige as in class for its last voyage. In class means compliance with rules and regulations. It does not mean the ship is safe or seaworthy. Insurance was with the London P&I Club, also called the London Club, a mutual association of shipowners.

Now the voyage. The Prestige began its journey from St. Petersburg in Russia, and according to the investigations it had not been properly inspected. From there it travelled through the Baltic Sea, a shallow and vulnerable sea, to the Atlantic. The trip was later questioned. Before this, in St. Petersburg, the ship's captain was Esfraitos Kostazos. He complained to the owners about several structural defects, but they rejected his complaints. In protest, Kostazos resigned. Why was the ship sent out despite these complaints? Instead of fixing the defects, the owners replaced Kostazos with Apostolos Mangouras. He was a Greek captain, and the crew was Filipino.

So the picture is an old single-hulled tanker, murky ownership, a rejected complaint and a new captain. But the story has another twist. Years earlier, a serious prediction had been made about two of the Prestige's sister ships. What was it?

articleEn: We have seen that the Prestige was a 26-year-old, structurally deficient tanker. The question now is how it reached the open sea. Here comes the most startling part of the story. Spanish investigators found that a hull failure like the Prestige's had been predicted before. The Prestige had two sister ships, the Alexandros and the Centaur, and there was a third sister ship called the Apanemo.

In 1996 the Alexandros and the Centaur went through extensive inspections under a program called Safe Hull. These inspections were the responsibility of the American Bureau of Shipping, the same ABS that was later the Prestige's classification society. ABS found that both the Alexandros and the Centaur were in terminal decline. In simple words, the ships were badly deteriorated. The cause was metal fatigue, meaning tiredness in the metal of the hull, which grows weak over time.

The modeling made a clear prediction: both ships would fail within five years between frames 61 and 71. Frames are parts of a ship's structure, so the danger was pointed to a very specific place, not a general one. Time passed. The Alexandros, the Centaur and the Apanemo were all scrapped between 1999 and 2002, which means those sister ships were removed from the sea. But the Prestige, another sister ship, kept working. At the time of the accident it was carrying 77,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil, and with such a cargo, a weak hull was a great danger.

Then came 13 November 2002. A little over five years after the sister-ship inspections, the Prestige's hull also failed between frames 61 and 71. After the failure, Serafin Diaz boarded the ship and saw a 15-metre hole on the starboard side. This was exactly the place the sister-ship warning had pointed to. Friends, was this only a coincidence, or a warning that was not taken seriously?

Now ABS's position. According to ABS, the ship took 6 days to break and sink in heavy seas, which proves it was not substandard. On the other side, Simon Walmsley of the World Wildlife Fund said most of the responsibility lies with the classification society. According to him, the ship had been reported as substandard at a port before reaching Spain. He wanted the whole inspection regime reformed and double-hulled tankers used. The shipping industry later debated whether classification societies could be held responsible, and this was called a potentially precedent-setting issue.

According to the investigations, the ship set out without a proper inspection, its ownership was unclear, and its hull failure had been predicted before. But so far we have looked only at the ship and the paperwork. The real test began on 13 November 2002, when a storm struck near the coast of Galicia.

articleEn: On 13 November 2002 the weather over the Atlantic had turned bad. A severe winter storm was blowing off Galicia in northwest Spain. This area is called Costa da Morte, which in English means Coast of Death. The name itself does not sound like a good omen. The Prestige was carrying 77,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil, two different grades of oil, in its tanks. The wind was strong and high waves were crashing against the ship. The ship was 26 years old and had a hull of only one layer.

Then suddenly a loud noise came from the starboard, or right, side of the ship. The Greek captain, Apostolos Mangouras, described it as a loud bang. After that, water began coming into the ship along with the high waves. Then the engines stopped as well, and the ship began to drift. Imagine it: a ship loaded with thousands of tonnes of oil, with dead engines and a coast a few kilometres away. What could the captain do but call for help?

Mangouras called Spanish rescue workers for help. That call was the first turning point of this story, because decisions were now going to be in the hands of the authorities. The Filipino crew was taken off the ship by rescue helicopter. Protecting human lives was the first priority, but the ship was still adrift. Wind and waves were slowly pushing it toward the coast, and at one point the Prestige was only 6 kilometres away.

Galicia is an environmentally important area. It has coral reefs, many kinds of sharks and birds, and its fishing industry is part of its identity. The problem was not only distance. The ship was already leaking oil, so pollution had started before it even reached the shore. Spanish authorities had to decide what to do with this helpless ship.

According to the Industry Ministry, an experienced captain was put aboard. His name was Serafín Díaz, a veteran captain. He was put on the ship to take it away from the Spanish coast toward the northwest. When Díaz reached the ship, he saw a big gash in the hull: a 15-metre, or 50-foot, open hole on the starboard side. Remember, this was the same kind of ship whose sister ships' inspections had already revealed the hull weakness.

The question now was where to take this wounded ship. Mangouras had one opinion and the Spanish authorities another. Three things were happening at once: the storm, the leaking oil and a difficult decision that grew bigger every hour. This event was later called the biggest environmental disaster in the history of Spain and Portugal. But it was only the first day. Díaz's job was to take the ship away from the coast, but Mangouras did not agree with this plan. Why? We look at that in the next part.

articleEn: Mangouras thought the ship should be taken to a port, arguing that the leaking oil could be contained there. But faced with a threat from the Spanish navy, he had to give up his view. So the decision to take the ship away from the coast, out to sea, went ahead. Here a question arises. The responsibility to grant a port of refuge has deep roots in history, so why was permission not given here? The answer lay in exemptions in international maritime law. If a ship could cause environmental or other damage to a port, the exemption can be used. The Spanish authorities applied this exemption.

The captain was ordered to restart the engines and take the ship offshore. Mangouras refused to follow this order. He was later arrested and faced criminal charges. The accusation was that he had not cooperated with marine salvage crews and had damaged the environment. But later the government's own decision was also questioned. Note one thing: the ownership of the ship was unclear, which later made it hard to decide who was liable.

Meanwhile the ship was being towed out to sea, but no safe place was being arranged. All three countries wanted it away from their coast. Then pressure came from France. The ship was turned south toward Portuguese waters, so that the southern coast of France would not be at risk. Now it was Portugal's turn. Fearing for its own coast, Portuguese authorities ordered the navy to stop the ailing ship and not let it advance. So France, Spain and Portugal all refused to let the Prestige dock. The ship had no shelter and no safe port, only open sea.

Friends, the scene was strange: an oil-laden tanker on one side, and three countries that did not want it to come close on the other. Was there a third way? For several days the ship was sometimes steered and sometimes towed, and the sea was rough. Then came 19 November. On 19 November 2002 the Prestige broke in two and sank. More than 64,000 m3 of oil escaped into the sea. The ship sank about 210 to 250 kilometres from the Spanish coast. Sources give both distances, so we are mentioning them together.

One more important point: an oil slick had already reached the coast before the ship sank. So the damage had already begun. The Spanish authorities were criticized because, instead of taking the ship into port, it was towed out to sea, where it broke into two pieces. Some people believe that bringing the ship into port and placing booms around it would have been less damaging. Some even called the decision a criminal act. On the other side, the authorities based their decision on the exemptions in maritime law. This same debate later reached the courts.

Fishing suspended six months (another source says bans over eight months, about 113 million euros compensation). Wreck leaking about 125 tonnes a day, toxicity concerns, comparison with Exxon Valdez, predicted ten years of harm to marine life.

articleEn: The ship had sunk, but the story was not over. The real damage was now about to show on Galicia and the nearby coasts. For Spain it became the country's biggest environmental disaster, and the environmental damage was greatest on the Galician coast. At first the government thought that only 17,000 tonnes of the ship's 77,000 tonnes of oil had been lost. The remaining roughly 60,000 tonnes, it believed, would solidify and not escape from the sunken tanker.

That estimate turned out to be wrong. In early 2003 the government admitted that half the oil had escaped, and by August 2003 the figure had reached about 63,000 tonnes. That means more than 80 percent of the 77,000 tonnes had spread into the sea near Spain's northwest coast. Sources give different figures: some say 60,000 tonnes or 67,000 m3, some 64,000 m3, and some 76,000 m3. The oil polluted 2,300 kilometres, or 1,429 miles, of coastline, and more than a thousand beaches in Spain, France and Portugal were affected. Think how large that distance is. It was not the coast of a single city but a coastline spread over three countries.

People's livelihoods depended on this coast. Galicia's regional government suspended offshore fishing for six months. According to another source, fishing restrictions lasted even more than eight months. Tax benefits and aid were given to reduce the loss, and about 113 million euros was spent on this help. Fishermen, ship owners and companies buying and selling fish were all affected by the ban. In general, the economic damage from a spill, in sectors like tourism and fishing, can be greater than the environmental damage. Fishing in Galicia became an example.

The problem did not stop at the sinking. After the sinking, about 125 tonnes of oil kept leaking from the wreck every day, and the seabed was polluted too. The wreck was very deep, and work on it comes later in the story.

Experts were also worried about the type of oil. It had light fractions containing polyaromatic hydrocarbons. According to experts, these materials could poison plankton, fish eggs and crustaceans. There was a fear of carcinogenic effects in fish, and possibly in humans too. Because of these fears, experts predicted that marine life could be affected by the pollution for at least ten years.

Now an important comparison. According to sources, the oil released from the Prestige was more than from the Exxon Valdez, and the environmental disaster was described as at least equal to it. According to one source, the toxicity of the Prestige's oil was also considered greater because the water temperature was higher. The danger was not only about quantity. So the real question was who would clean such a huge area, and what would happen to the oil lying on the seabed.

articleEn: The answer came in the form of thousands of volunteers. Ordinary people came forward along the Galician coast and arrived to help clean the affected shore. The public company TRAGSA, chosen by the regional government for the cleanup, also worked alongside them. Over the following months it became a big campaign. According to sources, most of the coast was restored by this campaign, and even older, everyday pollution was cleaned too.

Protest began along with the cleanup. Galician activists formed the Nunca Máis movement, meaning never again, to raise their voice against the government's inactive attitude. A year later an interesting thing came to light: Galicia's beaches received more Blue Flags than in earlier years. This is a world-class standard award.

But the oil lying on the seabed was still a problem. The wreck was 4,000 metres deep, and reaching it was not easy. In 2004 remotely operated vehicles, or ROVs, went to work. A vehicle like these had explored the wreck of the Titanic. The ROVs drilled small holes in the wreck, and then they began to pump out the remaining cargo oil, 13,000 cubic meters of it. The oil was filled into large aluminium shuttles specially made for the job, and the filled shuttles were then floated up to the surface. The first plan was to fill the oil into big bags, but that method turned out to be very problematic and slow, so it was dropped.

The ROVs also sealed cracks in the hull. As a result, the leakage was reduced to an ordinary flow of only 20 litres a day. Finally, a slurry rich in microbiologic agents was pumped into the wreck's hold so that the remaining oil would break down quickly. The cost of this whole operation was estimated at more than 100 million euros.

But did the story end here? In March 2006 new oil slicks appeared near the wreck. Researchers found that it was the same type of oil the Prestige had been carrying. Then in December 2006 a study led by physicist José Luis De Pablos came out. According to it, 16,000 to 23,000 tonnes of oil remained in the wreck. The Spanish government's claim was much lower, only 700 to 1,300 tonnes. The study also said that bioremediation had failed. According to the study, bacteria that corrode the hull could soon cause ruptures, so it appealed to the government for prompt action.

Meanwhile Spain's Council of Ministers approved Plan Galicia on 23 January 2003. It was a series of economic measures to reduce the effects of the disaster. In a 2003 report, Galicia's Barrie de la Maza economic institute criticized the government's handling. Its estimate was that the cost of cleaning just the Galician coast reached 2.5 billion euros.

And finally, a memorial. In 2003 Alberto Bañuelos's sculpture A Ferida, meaning the wound, was installed. It is dedicated to the volunteers who cleaned tar off the beaches. This 400-ton monument is the biggest sculpture in Spain. Now the question was who was responsible, and who would pay the bill.

articleEn: Who was responsible? There were different views. Simon Walmsley of the World Wildlife Fund believed that most of the blame falls on the classification society. He said the ship had been reported as substandard at a port before reaching Spain. In his view the whole inspection regime should change, and double-hulled tankers should be used. ABS had a different position. According to it, the ship took 6 days to break and sink, which is proof positive that it was not substandard. The Spanish government's decision to tow the ship was also criticized. Refusing the ship shelter in a port was called a major reason for the scale of the disaster.

Could the courts solve this tangle? In May 2003 Spain filed a civil suit against ABS in a New York court. ABS is a Houston-based classification society, and it had declared the Prestige in class for its last voyage. Spain's initial claim was about 700 million dollars. But the case was dismissed. The judge said that ABS is a person under the CLC convention and is therefore exempt from direct liability for pollution damage.

Then came the stage in Spain's own court. In the High Court of Galicia, 133 witnesses and 98 experts were heard during the trial. But in November 2013 the three judges said that criminal responsibility could not be proved. Captain Mangouras was acquitted of crimes against the environment. However, he was found guilty of disobeying government authorities and received a nine-month suspended sentence. According to the court, the decision to keep the tanker away from the coast was correct.

Spain appealed, and on 26 January 2016 the Supreme Court found Mangouras guilty of recklessness and sentenced him to two years in prison. After this conviction, far larger compensation claims against the insurers became possible. The Supreme Court held the London P&I Club liable up to a limit of 1 billion dollars. In 2017 a court in A Coruña awarded damages of a little over 1.5 billion euros, which the Supreme Court confirmed in December 2018.

The insurer did not take part in the Spanish proceedings, because under the contract the matter was to be settled by arbitration in England. In 2013 a tribunal accepted its position. In October 2023 the English High Court refused to enforce the Spanish ruling on the basis of the arbitration terms. This decision was also upheld by the Court of Appeal and the UK Supreme Court. So the ruling could not be enforced in England.

Now, what changed? The European Commissioner for Transport, Spain's Loyola de Palacio, pushed for a ban on single-hulled tankers. According to sources, tankers like the Prestige were afterward kept away from the French and Spanish coastlines. The US and most other countries were planning to phase out single-hulled tankers by 2012. According to one source, the 1992 amendment to MARPOL made double hulls mandatory for tankers of 5,000 dwt and above.

So, friends, questions remain at the end. Who was responsible for the condition of the ship? How good was the decision to send it away from the coast? And were the lessons really learned? shorts.titleEn: The Warning About the Prestige That Came 5 Years Early
shorts.text: کیا ایک جہاز کی ناکامی کی پیش گوئی پانچ سال پہلے ہی ہو چکی تھی؟ 1996 میں Prestige کے دو sister ships، Alexandros اور Centaur، کی extensive inspections ہوئیں۔ یہ inspections "Safe Hull" program کے تحت American Bureau of Shipping یعنی ABS نے کیں۔ وہی ABS جو Prestige کی classification society بھی تھی۔ ABS نے پایا کہ دونوں جہاز terminal decline میں ہیں۔ Metal fatigue کی وجہ سے modeling نے بتایا کہ پانچ سال کے اندر دونوں کی hull frames 61 اور 71 کے درمیان ناکام ہو جائے گی۔ Alexandros، Centaur اور تیسرا sister ship Apanemo 1999 سے 2002 کے درمیان scrap کر دیے گئے۔ مگر Prestige چلتا رہا۔ پھر پانچ سال سے کچھ زیادہ بعد، Prestige کی hull بالکل اسی جگہ، frames 61 اور 71 کے درمیان، ناکام ہو گئی۔ کیا یہ صرف اتفاق تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya ek jahaz ki nakami ki paish goi paanch saal pehle hi ho chuki thi? 1996 mein Prestige ke do sister ships, Alexandros aur Centaur, ki extensive inspections huin. Yeh inspections "Safe Hull" program ke tehat American Bureau of Shipping yani ABS ne keen. Wohi ABS jo Prestige ki classification society bhi thi. ABS ne paya ke dono jahaz terminal decline mein hain. Metal fatigue ki wajah se modeling ne bataya ke paanch saal ke andar dono ki hull frames 61 aur 71 ke darmiyan nakam ho jayegi. Alexandros, Centaur aur teesra sister ship Apanemo 1999 se 2002 ke darmiyan scrap kar diye gaye. Magar Prestige chalta raha. Phir paanch saal se kuch zyada baad, Prestige ki hull bilkul isi jagah, frames 61 aur 71 ke darmiyan, nakam ho gayi. Kya yeh sirf ittefaq tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: In 1996 inspectors predicted the hull failure of the Prestige's sister ships. The Prestige failed in the same spot, a little over five years later.

shorts.titleEn: The Bang Off the Coast of Death: 13 November 2002
shorts.text: جس سمندر کا نام ہی Coast of Death ہو، وہاں طوفان آ جائے تو کیا ہوگا؟ 13 November 2002۔ Spain کے شمال مغرب میں Galicia کے قریب ایک سخت winter storm چل رہا تھا۔ Prestige اس وقت 77,000 tonnes heavy fuel oil لے کر جا رہا تھا۔ یہ دو مختلف grades کا تیل تھا۔ اچانک جہاز کی starboard طرف سے زوردار آواز آئی۔ Greek captain Apostolos Mangouras نے اسے loud bang بتایا۔ اونچی لہروں کے ساتھ جہاز میں پانی بھرنے لگا اور engines بند ہو گئے۔ Captain نے Spanish rescue workers سے مدد مانگی۔ Crew کو helicopters کے ذریعے نکال لیا گیا۔ جہاز بہتا ہوا Spanish coast سے صرف 6 کلومیٹر کے فاصلے تک پہنچ گیا، اور اس سے تیل پہلے ہی رس رہا تھا۔ اب سوال یہ تھا کہ اس جہاز کا کیا کیا جائے؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Jis samandar ka naam hi Coast of Death ho, wahan toofan aa jaye to kya hoga? 13 November 2002. Spain ke shumal maghrib mein Galicia ke qareeb ek sakht winter storm chal raha tha. Prestige us waqt 77,000 tonnes heavy fuel oil le kar ja raha tha. Yeh do mukhtalif grades ka tel tha. Achanak jahaz ki starboard taraf se zordaar awaaz aayi. Greek captain Apostolos Mangouras ne ise loud bang bataya. Unchi lehron ke saath jahaz mein pani bharne laga aur engines band ho gaye. Captain ne Spanish rescue workers se madad mangi. Crew ko helicopters ke zariye nikal liya gaya. Jahaz behta hua Spanish coast se sirf 6 kilometre ke faasle tak pahunch gaya, aur is se tel pehle hi ris raha tha. Ab sawal yeh tha ke is jahaz ka kya kiya jaye? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: On 13 November 2002 a storm off Galicia's Coast of Death left the Prestige drifting 6 km from shore. The crew was evacuated and oil was already leaking.

shorts.titleEn: Robots Drilled a Wreck 4,000 Metres Under the Sea
shorts.text: سمندر کی سطح سے 4000 میٹر نیچے ایک wreck سے تیل کیسے نکالا جائے؟ Prestige ڈوبنے کے بعد بھی روزانہ تقریباً 125 tonnes تیل چھوڑ رہا تھا۔ 2004 میں ROVs، یعنی remotely operated vehicles، میدان میں آئیں۔ ویسی ہی ایک ROV نے RMS Titanic کا wreck بھی explore کیا تھا۔ انہوں نے wreck میں چھوٹے سوراخ کیے اور باقی 13,000 m3 cargo oil نکالا۔ یہ تیل بڑے aluminium shuttles میں بھرا گیا، جو خاص اسی کام کے لیے بنائے گئے تھے۔ پھر یہ shuttles تیرتے ہوئے سطح پر آئے۔ بڑے bags والا اصل منصوبہ بہت سست اور مشکل نکلا تھا۔ ROVs نے hull کی دراڑیں بھی بند کیں، اور leakage گھٹ کر صرف 20 litres روزانہ رہ گئی۔ اس پورے operation پر 100 million euros سے زیادہ خرچ آیا۔ مگر آخر میں wreck کے اندر ایک اور چیز پمپ کی گئی۔ وہ کیا تھی؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Samandar ki satah se 4000 meter neeche ek wreck se tel kaise nikala jaye? Prestige doobne ke baad bhi rozana taqriban 125 tonnes tel chhod raha tha. 2004 mein ROVs, yani remotely operated vehicles, maidan mein aayin. Waisi hi ek ROV ne RMS Titanic ka wreck bhi explore kiya tha. Unhon ne wreck mein chhote surakh kiye aur baqi 13,000 m3 cargo oil nikala. Yeh tel bade aluminium shuttles mein bhara gaya, jo khaas isi kaam ke liye banaye gaye thay. Phir yeh shuttles tairte hue satah par aaye. Bade bags wala asal mansooba bohat sust aur mushkil nikla tha. ROVs ne hull ki dararen bhi band keen, aur leakage ghat kar sirf 20 litres rozana reh gayi. Is poore operation par 100 million euros se zyada kharch aaya. Magar aakhir mein wreck ke andar ek aur cheez pump ki gayi. Woh kya thi? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: In 2004 ROVs removed the remaining cargo oil from the Prestige wreck, 4,000 metres down. The operation cost over 100 million euros.
